claims.text: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the stability of the high-temperature BCC phase is governed by the onset of chemical short-range order during cooling.
Below a critical order-disorder transition temperature, preferential Cr–Al interactions lower the free energy of locally ordered configurations.
Formation of locally ordered configurations destabilizes the disordered BCC phase.
Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can initially be prepared as a single-phase BCC alloy at high temperature or in the as-cast condition.
Annealing at temperatures such as 600°C and 800°C while holding composition, atmosphere, and hold time constant provides a controlled comparison across the proposed SRO onset.
Chemical SRO clusters eventually act as nuclei for transformation into ordered phases such as B2.
At elevated temperature, configurational entropy stabilizes the homogeneous BCC phase.
Attractive interactions between Cr and Al drive SRO formation during cooling.
Once SRO reaches a critical threshold near the order-disorder transition, ordered arrangements further reduce local free energy.
The free-energy reduction caused by ordering triggers secondary-phase nucleation and instability of the BCC matrix.
Samples annealed below the critical temperature will exhibit diffuse-scattering signatures of SRO.
Samples annealed below the critical temperature will exhibit nanoscale compositional modulation detectable by TEM or atom-probe tomography.
Samples annealed below the critical temperature will subsequently form ordered precipitates.
Samples maintained above the order-disorder transition temperature will retain a uniform BCC structure.
The proposed mechanism operates within a temperature window around the order-disorder transition.
Cooling rate can alter the observable phase evolution by changing ordering and transformation kinetics.
Small changes in Al or Cr content can alter the thermodynamic driving force for ordering.
The critical SRO-onset temperature and the stoichiometry and structure of the ensuing ordered precipitates are not quantitatively established.
Diffusion kinetics may modify the observable phase evolution.
The hypothesis is falsified if below-ODTT samples show no measurable increase in SRO indicators or secondary-phase formation relative to above-ODTT samples.
